## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no results yet, and scores stay hidden, so later rounds can only tell whether a trial ran, not how well it did. Each candidate should therefore be a strong guess, and the three should differ. The budget is tight: the default settings give only 32 updates (131k steps of 4,096 each), so more frequent policy updates could matter as much as the network. The starting network decides each placement from max/min/avg pools of features over the brick's footprint. It cannot easily express the actual rule for a good placement: the brick lands at layer L = max build height under it; it is good if the target fills every footprint cell at L and nothing still missing is left below L, where it would be sealed in. A head that keeps a separate layer for each height, pools over the footprint, then reduces over height can express this directly. Candidates: (1) the starting network with more frequent updates and a longer horizon; (2) the per-layer landing head; (3) a deeper network with global context added back into every cell.

### Round 2
Scores are hidden, so the only things we know are that all three round-1 trials trained without errors and passed the checks. Nothing shows which idea helped. The bets stay spread out, and each new trial changes one thing compared with an earlier one. On an 8x8 grid most placement decisions are local: what lies under the footprint and what is still missing below. Two global questions are harder for the network: when to choose DONE, and the order in which to build overhangs. Round 1 used 2.4 to 4.1x fewer samples than PPO epochs alone would allow, so cutting to 2 epochs nearly doubles the samples. That is worth testing on its own (A) and on the per-layer landing head, which got few samples in round 1 (C). The third trial adds one cheap self-attention block over the 64 cells, using the recipe from r1c1 so the attention is the only difference (B).

### Round 3
Scores are hidden, so nothing so far shows which trials did better. All six trials trained without errors. Two changed only the recipe on the starting network: r1c1 used 3 epochs (162k steps) and r2c1 used 2 epochs (229k steps). Three new networks were tried. The per-layer landing head ran twice (100k and 188k steps). The deeper network with a grid summary (94k steps) and the attention block (119k steps) each ran only once, on fewer samples. With fresh designs every episode, more samples are probably worth more than reusing each sample. So the most useful step now is to run the less-tested networks with the 2-epoch recipe that gives more samples, and separately to push the sample count about 3x higher with a single epoch. Without scores, the final choice rests on the real dev results. The aim is to give the selection several strong, different candidates.

### Round 4
No scores are visible, so I can only reason about design. All 9 trials ran without errors. r3c2 (about 400k steps) shows that 1 PPO epoch with 512 envs fits within the time limit. Three ideas have each been tried at 2 or 3 epochs but never with 1 epoch: per-layer landing heads, cell attention, and more samples per unit of compute. Since this is the last round, I will put these ideas together rather than open new directions. A and B test whether attention or the landing head works best with lots of samples at 1 epoch. C combines both modules at 2 epochs, which hedges in case 1 epoch is too few gradient steps. For the 1-epoch runs I use 32 minibatches instead of 16, which doubles the gradient steps per update compared with r3c2.
